questions.q: The prognosis of Salter-Harris Type III and Type IV is:
questions.exp: Type III: prognosis bad. Type IV: prognosis bad (growth impacted even on reducing the fracture). (Book p156)

questions.q: In Salter-Harris Type IV:
opts: The fracture line goes through all layers; germinal layer injured; growth impacted even on reducing the fracture
The fracture line goes only towards the metaphysis
questions.exp: Type IV: fracture line through all layers; germinal layer injured; growth is impacted even on reducing the fracture. (Book p156)

questions.q: Fracture of the lower end of tibia is an example of Salter-Harris Type:
questions.exp: Type III example: fracture of lower end of tibia. (Book p156)

questions.q: Lateral condyle of humerus fracture is an example of Salter-Harris Type:
questions.exp: Type IV example: lateral condyle of humerus fracture. (Book p156)

questions.q: Salter-Harris Type V is best described as:
opts: An impaction injury that crushes the growth plate
questions.exp: Type V: impaction injury -> crushes growth plate. (Book p156)

questions.q: Salter-Harris Type V injury is classically:
opts: Missed on X-ray - retrospective diagnosis, with late presentation as limb length discrepancy
questions.exp: Type V: fracture is missed on X-ray; retrospective diagnosis; late presentation with limb length discrepancy. (Book p156)

questions.q: The worst prognosis in the Salter-Harris classification belongs to Type:
questions.exp: Type V: prognosis worst. (Book p156)

questions.q: Fall from height is an example of Salter-Harris Type:
questions.exp: Type V example: fall from height. (Book p156)

questions.q: Congenital muscular torticollis is also known as:
questions.exp: Congenital muscular torticollis / wry neck. (Book p157)

questions.q: In congenital muscular torticollis, the head is tilted to one side and it most commonly occurs on the:
questions.exp: Tilting of head to one side; most commonly occurs on right side. (Book p157)

questions.q: The etiology of congenital muscular torticollis is birth trauma of the:
questions.exp: Etiology: birth trauma of sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle. (Book p157)

questions.q: All of the following are risk factors for SCM birth trauma EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Risk factors: breech presentation, shoulder dystocia, forceps delivery. (Book p157)

questions.q: In the pathogenesis of congenital muscular torticollis:
opts: Contraction and ischemia of SCM -> necrosis and fibrosis -> contracture, causing neck tilt
questions.exp: Pathogenesis: contraction of SCM -> neck tilt; ischemia of SCM -> necrosis and fibrosis -> contracture. (Book p157)

questions.q: The contracture in congenital muscular torticollis is located:
opts: At the upper pole of the SCM
At the junction of upper 2/3rd and lower 1/3rd, affecting the clavicular head of SCM
Along the entire length of the muscle
questions.exp: Contracture at junction of upper 2/3rd and lower 1/3rd; affects clavicular head of SCM. (Book p157)

questions.q: Soon after birth, the clinical feature of congenital muscular torticollis is:
questions.exp: Only head tilt is appreciated soon after birth. (Book p157)

questions.q: The fibrotic mass that may be palpated 3 months after birth in congenital muscular torticollis is called:
questions.exp: Fibrotic mass maybe palpated 3 months after birth (SCM tumor). (Book p157)

questions.q: Conservative treatment of congenital muscular torticollis is:
opts: Gradual stretching of the neck -> corrects itself; most cases are self resolving
questions.exp: Conservative: gradual stretching of the neck -> corrects itself; most cases are self resolving. (Book p157)

questions.q: Surgical release of congenital muscular torticollis is done:
opts: If not corrected by 1 year of age
questions.exp: Surgical release: if not corrected by 1 year of age. (Book p157)

questions.q: If congenital muscular torticollis is not corrected by 1 year of age, the complication is:
opts: Plagiocephaly (head grows in an abnormal direction)
questions.exp: If not corrected by 1 year of age -> plagiocephaly (head grows in an abnormal direction). (Book p157)

questions.q: The acquired causes of torticollis include:
opts: Vision problems, extra ocular muscle palsy
questions.exp: Note: acquired causes of torticollis: vision problems, extra ocular muscle palsy. (Book p157)

questions.q: Sprengel's deformity is a:
questions.exp: Sprengel's deformity: congenital undescended hypoplastic scapula. (Book p157)

questions.q: Sprengel's deformity is associated with:
questions.exp: Sprengel's deformity is associated with Klippel Feil syndrome. (Book p157)

questions.q: The etiology of Sprengel's deformity is the presence of an omovertebral bar, which:
questions.exp: Etiology: presence of omovertebral bar -> prevents scapular descent. (Book p157)

questions.q: The features of Sprengel's deformity include:
opts: Both scapulae at the same level
One scapula at a higher level than the other, with restricted movement of the affected shoulder
questions.exp: Features: one scapula at a higher level than the other; restricted movement of affected shoulder. (Book p158)

questions.q: Treatment of Sprengel's deformity is the Woodward operation, performed:
questions.exp: Treatment: Woodward operation (between 3-8 years of age). (Book p158)

questions.q: If the Woodward operation is done after 8 years of age, the risk is:
questions.exp: If done after 8 years of age -> neural traction injury. (Book p158)

questions.q: Klippel Feil syndrome is caused by:
questions.exp: Cause: segmentation defect of cervical vertebrae. (Book p158)

questions.q: Features of Klippel Feil syndrome include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Features: short webbed neck, restriction of neck movements, low set hair line. (Book p158)

questions.q: Klippel Feil syndrome has a strong association with:
questions.exp: Klippel Feil syndrome: strong association with scoliosis. (Book p158)

questions.q: Madelung deformity is characterized by:
opts: Ulna radial mismatch, with 50% cases bilateral
questions.exp: Madelung deformity: ulna radial mismatch; 50% cases are bilateral. (Book p158)

questions.q: The etiopathogenesis of Madelung deformity is a defect in the growth plate of the distal end of the radius, causing:
opts: Affected radius growth with normal ulna growth
questions.exp: Defect in the growth plate of distal end of radius: affects radius growth; normal ulna growth -> ulna radial mismatch. (Book p158)

questions.q: The clinical features of Madelung deformity include:
opts: Prominent ulna dorsally, with dinner fork deformity in children
questions.exp: Clinical features: prominent ulna dorsally; dinner fork deformity in children. (Book p158)

questions.q: The treatment of Madelung deformity is Darrach's procedure:
opts: Resection of terminal end of radius
questions.exp: Darrach's procedure: resect terminal end of ulna. (Book p158)

questions.q: Amelia refers to:
opts: Both long and short bones absent / complete absence of limb
Long bones absent, short bones present
questions.exp: Amelia: both long and short bones absent / complete absence of limb. (Book p158)

questions.q: Phocomelia is characterized by:
opts: Absence of both long and short bones
Long bones absent, short bones present
questions.exp: Phocomelia: long bones absent, short bones present. (Book p158)

questions.q: The cause of phocomelia is:
questions.exp: Cause: thalidomide. (Book p158)

questions.q: Hemi-melia refers to:
questions.exp: Hemi-melia: longitudinal deficiency of limb. (Book p159)

questions.q: The m/c type of hemi-melia is:
questions.exp: M/c: fibular hemimelia. (Book p159)

questions.q: In tibial hemimelia, the bone that is absent is the:
questions.exp: Tibial hemimelia: tibia is absent. (Book p159)

questions.q: Radial hemimelia (radial club hand) is d/t:
opts: Absent radius - longitudinal deficiency of radial side of limb
questions.exp: Radial hemimelia / radial club hand: absent radius; longitudinal deficiency of radial side of limb. (Book p159)

questions.q: Associated syndromes of hemi-melia include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Associated syndromes: Holt-Oram, Fanconi, TAR, Vacter syndrome. (Book p159)

questions.q: Cleidocranial dysostosis is characterized by:
opts: Abnormality in skull and clavicle, with congenital absence of clavicle
questions.exp: Cleidocranial dysostosis: abnormality in skull and clavicle; congenital absence of clavicle. (Book p159)

questions.q: A distinctive feature of cleidocranial dysostosis is that the shoulders:
opts: Can be brought close to each other
questions.exp: Shoulders can be brought close to each other. (Book p159)

questions.q: Poland syndrome is a congenital absence of muscle; the m/c is absence of the:
questions.exp: Poland syndrome: congenital absence of muscle; m/c: pectoralis muscle absence. (Book p159)

units.title: Characteristics of Paediatric Bones
units.guide: The child's bone is wetter, springier and wrapped in a thick periosteum: it bends rather than breaks, and the metaphysis can remodel deformities that would stay permanent in an adult. Water content, thick periosteum and remodeling potential are the paediatric skeleton's three gifts.

units.title: Force, Greenstick & Torus
units.guide: Bend the child's bone within physiological limits and it bows: the outer convex surface takes tension, the inner concave surface compression. Push past the limit and either the outer cortex breaks - a greenstick, like the stem of a growing tree, m/c in the radius, treated by osteoclasis of the intact cortex - or the inner surface buckles into a torus, a tubular cylinder at the base of a pillar, settled by a simple POP.

units.title: Commonest Fractures
units.guide: Three 'commonest' lines to hold: at birth the clavicle fractures, after a fall on an outstretched hand it is the supracondylar humerus, and overall the commonest fracture is still the clavicle.

units.title: Toddler's Fracture
units.guide: A toddler's fracture is a spiral, undisplaced tibial fracture from a trivial accident; the thick periosteum supports it, the intact fibula lets the child still walk on it with a painful limp, and a POP cast is all it needs.

units.title: Battered Baby Syndrome
units.guide: A shaken child leaves metaphyseal bruises - bucket handle fractures from violent to-and-fro shaking in children under 2, avulsing the capsule from the bone. Multiple fractures in different stages of healing, an inconsistent history with neglect, and long bone fractures in a non-ambulatory child send the X-ray scanogram out.

units.title: Growth Plate Injuries
units.guide: Growth marches from epiphysis to metaphysis through five layers: germinal (most important, the chondrocyte stem cells), proliferative, hypertrophic (weakest), calcification and ossification. Damage the germinal layer and you damage the future - at the knee, partial damage restricts the medial condyle and the leg bows into genu varus.

units.title: Salter-Harris: Types I & II
units.guide: The Salter-Harris ladder starts gently: Type I splits the plate without touching the germinal layer (SCFE), and Type II - the m/c - adds a Thurston Holland metaphyseal fragment, as in supracondylar humerus fractures. Both spare the germinal layer, both grow normally on reduction, both carry a good prognosis.

units.title: Salter-Harris: Types III-V
units.guide: From Type III upward the germinal layer burns: III runs toward the epiphysis (lower end of tibia), IV crosses every layer (lateral condyle of humerus) and both have a bad prognosis. Type V is the silent one - impaction crushes the plate, X-ray misses it, and it announces itself late as limb length discrepancy after a fall from height: the worst prognosis of all.

units.title: Congenital Muscular Torticollis
units.guide: The wry neck starts as a birth injury to the SCM - breech, shoulder dystocia, forceps; ischemia turns the junction of its upper 2/3rd and lower 1/3rd, at the clavicular head, into a fibrotic cord. The head tilts, most often to the right; by 3 months the SCM tumor is palpable. Stretching corrects most cases themselves; miss the 1-year mark and it is surgical release - and an uncorrected year invites plagiocephaly. Acquired torticollis hides in vision problems and extra ocular muscle palsy.

units.title: Sprengel's Deformity
units.guide: In Sprengel's deformity the scapula never finished descending - an omovertebral bar held it - so it sits high and hypoplastic with a stiff shoulder, often alongside Klippel Feil's webbed neck. The Woodward operation frees it between 3 and 8 years; done after 8, neural traction injury becomes the new problem.

units.title: Klippel Feil & Madelung
units.guide: Klippel Feil is a segmentation defect of the cervical vertebrae: short webbed neck, low hair line, restricted movement, strong association with scoliosis. Madelung is the wrist's growth-plate failure: the distal radius stalls while the ulna keeps growing, the ulna crowds dorsally in the dinner fork deformity, and Darrach's procedure resects the terminal ulna.

units.title: Limb Deficiency
units.guide: Limb deficiency comes in three grades: amelia (both long and short bones absent - complete absence of limb), phocomelia (long bones absent, short bones present - thalidomide's signature), and hemi-melia, the longitudinal deficiency where the fibula is the m/c absentee (tibial hemimelia, or the absent radius of radial club hand). Holt-Oram, Fanconi, TAR and Vacter are its syndromic company.

units.title: Miscellaneous
units.guide: Two rare pearls: cleidocranial dysostosis, with its skull and clavicle abnormality, congenitally absent clavicle and shoulders that can be brought close together; and Poland syndrome, the congenital absence of muscle, most often the pectoralis.
